newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia, NZ forge single aviation market.
newsitem.headline: Australia, NZ forge single aviation market.

text.p: Australia and New Zealand on Thursday sealed the merger of their air transport systems into a single A$5.0 billion (US$4.0 billion) aviation market.
Under the single aviation market agreement, airlines of both countries have unrestricted rights to fly anywhere in the other country.

"The arrangement will create a new market worth an estimated A$5.0 billion and covering more than 31 million passengers a year, by bringing together the domestic travel markets of each country and the trans-Tasman market which links them," Australian Transport Minister John Sharp said.
Sharp said he hoped the increased competition from the new market would spark fare cuts of at least five percent.
"I'd like to think the figure would be greater, but I would be reluctant to speculate," he said.
Sharp said there would be no limit on the number of airlines from either country that could operate services within the single aviation market.
The agreement, which comes into force on November 1, did not include rights for New Zealand carriers to fly beyond Australia, but Sharp said the governments were now considering the move.

"We are very aware of the interest that New Zealand has in this and we are now negotiating with the New Zealand government over beyond rights," he said, adding that Australian air operators would also be consulted.
Single aviation market discussions began in 1992, but Australia's former Labor government transport minister Laurie Brereton cancelled the plan shortly before it was due to come into effect in 1994.

Brereton cited the single aviation market's impact on the value of the Australian national flag carrier Qantas Airways Ltd, then 75 percent government-owned, as the reason for the last-minute decision.
Australia's new Liberal-National government promised before it won this year's March 2 election to restore the deal.
"We have restored our relationship with New Zealand and repaired the damage done by the previous government's last minute axing of the agreement," Sharp said.
To be eligible to operate in the single market, airlines are required to have at least 50 percent ownership and effective board control by nationals of Australia, New Zealand or both.
Two-thirds of the board, including the chairperson, must also be Australians, New Zealanders or both. The airlines must have a head office and operational base in Australia or New Zealand.
Approved carriers are Ansett New Zealand, Air New Zealand, Ansett Australia and Qantas Airways.
Air New Zealand is buying Australian transport group TNT Ltd's 50 percent stake in Ansett's domestic Australian operation.
Rupert Murdoch's media firm News Corp, which holds the other 50 percent in Ansett Australia, will assume full ownership of the New Zealand domestic operator, Ansett New Zealand.
Ansett Australia welcomed the move, saying it also expected the agreement to result in lower fares.
"Ansett has always supported the concept of a single aviation market, so we welcome the decision of both governments to open the trans-Tasman market," spokeswoman Jane Corbett-Jones told Reuters.
"We see competition on that route or any route as being beneficial to passengers and carriers alike," she said.
